bib.title: HeavySkill: Heavy Thinking as the Inner Skill in Agentic Harness

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "HeavySkill: Heavy Thinking as the Inner Skill in Agentic Harness", Jianing Wang et al. (Meituan LongCat Team; one author also at Peking University). Preprint, arXiv 2605.02396v1, 4–5 May 2026. Code is at github.com/wjn1996/HeavySkill.

COVERAGE: 18 of 18 pages, all 70,512 characters, including the appendices, the skill file and the prompt. The references were skimmed. Tables and figures extracted cleanly.

CORE CLAIM
- The authors argue that what drives performance in orchestrated harnesses (subagents, skills, memory) is one model capability, "heavy thinking". It is a two-stage pipeline: K parallel reasoning trajectories, then one deliberation pass that synthesises them.
- They ship this pipeline as a plain-text skill file (Figs 8–10) that the orchestrator reads and runs itself. They say the same file ran unchanged in Claude Code and in a custom harness.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
All of these use temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 10, N=1 iteration, K in {8,16}, and 4 summaries per problem (HM@4). Both stages use the same model unless stated. The paper reports no seeds, error bars or run counts. Small benchmarks are scored from single sampled sets, and AIME25 and HMMT25 have only 30 problems each.
- **Table 1, STEM.** Heavy-Mean@4 (HM@4) beats mean single-trajectory accuracy (Mean@K) for every model listed. It does not always beat plain majority vote (Vote@K). Examples at K=8:
  - GPT-5 Thinking, AIME25: Vote 96.7, HM 96.7.
  - Claude 4.5 Thinking, BeyondAIME: Vote 66.0, HM 63.3.
  - Kimi K2 Thinking, HMMT: Vote 90.0, HM 93.3.
  - Kimi K2 Thinking, GPQA-Diamond: Vote 82.3, HM 86.9.
- **Pass@K ceiling.** HM@4 usually stays below Pass@K. Heavy-Pass@4 exceeds Pass@K "in nearly half" of trials (p.5). Example: IMO-AnswerBench, GLM 4.6, HP@4 86.0 against P@K 89.5 in Table 2, which contradicts the text's claim of 86.0 vs 75.1.
- **Table 2, general tasks.**
  - Gains: GPT-OSS-20B on IMO-AnswerBench, 65.8 to 71.0. Kimi K2 on IMO-AnswerBench, 69.1 to 77.2.
  - Mixed: Arena-Hard shows marginal or slightly negative change.
  - Text-versus-table inconsistencies: the text says GPT-OSS-20B LiveCodeBench goes "69.7% to 85.5%", but the table shows HM@4 69.2 and HP@4 85.5, so 85.5 is the pass figure, not the mean. The text also says R1-Distill-Qwen-32B IFEval goes 35.7 to 69.3, but the table row is R1-Distill-Qwen3-8B.
- **Table 3, tool use.** Python interpreter, 50 rounds maximum. HM@4 beats Vote@4 in 5 of 6 cells, with Qwen3-32B on AIME25 (83.3 vote against 80.0 heavy) the exception, although the text says "consistently". GPT-OSS-20B on AIME25: 90.0 heavy against 83.3 vote.
- **Sec 4.1 (R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, 10k queries, K=16).** Of queries with parallel pass rate below 0.5, "over 500" were rescued and about 1,400 stayed unresolved. Above 0.5, accuracy stayed above 98%, with about 30 queries degraded.
- **Sec 4.2.** The deliberator can be a different model. With R1-Distill-Qwen-7B generating, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct as deliberator still beat Mean@K. Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct itself scores 12.8% on AIME25.
- **Sec 4.3.** Over 4 iterations, HM@K rises but HP@K falls. Fig 4 is read only as a plot.

QUOTES
- "we abstract the agentic harness into the LLM's inherent capability of heavy thinking." (p.1)
- "heavy thinking is not an artifact of a particular system design but an inner skill that can be activated across diverse orchestration environments." (p.4)
- "A skill specifies when to activate, how to execute, and what to output, without requiring any code modification to the harness itself." (p.3)
- "the sequential deliberation phase does not necessarily demand peak intrinsic reasoning power from the model." (p.7)

LIMITS AND WHAT IS NOT SHOWN
- **No harness-versus-model comparison.** Every experiment is a Python workflow, not a skill running in a real harness.
  - Portability to Claude Code is asserted ("We have verified", p.4) with no data.
  - The skill file recommends K=3–5, while all results use K=8 or 16.
  - The paper never compares a harness with and without the skill.
- **Narrow task scope.** The benchmarks are STEM, code and instruction following, with verifiable answers.
  - The paper itself says gains are weaker on preference-style tasks (Arena-Hard).
  - It does not examine agentic, long-horizon or software-engineering tasks.
  - It gives no cost accounting: heavy thinking costs roughly K+1 times the tokens, and the paper has no compute-matched baselines beyond voting.
- **Contradicts its own framing.** The abstract says heavy thinking is learnable and "without relying on brittle orchestration layers". It also says RL scaling is shown, but the main text has no RL section and gives no numbers. Only Fig 6 (p.14) shows curves, in an appendix with a one-line caption.
- **Weak support for the harness claim.** The "abstract the agentic harness into heavy thinking" claim is a thesis, not a demonstration. Table 1 shows gains from best-of-K plus synthesis, which is a known test-time-scaling result. The paper does not show that real orchestrators work this way.
- **Draft quality.** It reads as an early preprint with typos, text/table mismatches, and missing cells (marked "-" in Table 1).

BUILDS ON
- Parallel reasoning and test-time scaling: Brown et al. 2024 (Large Language Monkeys), Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023), Parallel-R1 (Zheng et al. 2025b), ParaThinker (Wen et al. 2025).
- The two-stage "parallel then deliberate" pattern: Kimi K2 (Bai et al. 2025), PaCoRe (StepFun-AI 2025), LongCat-Flash-Thinking-2601 (Wang et al. 2026).
- The skills concept: Claude Code skills, citing Xu & Yan 2026 (Agent skills survey).
- Training: RLVR as in DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al. 2025), DAPO (Yu et al. 2025), VeRL.

FIGURE CANDIDATE
Fig 1 (p.3), "The overview framework of heavy thinking in LLMs test time scaling". It shows query, K parallel thinkers, memory cache, deliberation, and optional iterative update.

FIT
- **Weak fit for 01-what-a-harness-is.** It does not define a harness, a ratchet, or the model-versus-harness split, and it does not test a skill-issue claim or per-model tuning.
- **Better fit for 07-orchestration** (parallel subagents plus a synthesis step; the note "do NOT delegate" deliberation).
- **Also fits 03-tool-design skills** (the anatomy of a skill file: activation, protocol, prompt, output constraints).
- If cited in 01, the only supportable use is as a narrow data point that the "skill" layer can be a prompt-level document with an inner reasoning pattern. Do not use it as evidence that the harness reduces to the model.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The text/table discrepancies listed above are in the source, not extraction faults.
